catalog_quote: ラヤ族の話すラヤ語 (Layakha) は、南部チベット語 (チベット語南部方言とも) の一つに分類されるゾンカ語 (Dzongkha) の一種であるが、構造的、語彙的にチベット語に近い特徴を持つ (Van Driem 1998)。ラヤ語には高低二種類の声調があるようである。本稿では、高声調は /ā/ のように母音に上線で、低声調は /a/ のように母音のみで示す。

new_statements.translation: Layakha, spoken by the Laya people, is classified as a variety of Dzongkha, one of the Southern Tibetan languages (also called southern Tibetan dialects), but it has features structurally and lexically close to Tibetan (van Driem 1998). Laya appears to have two tones, high and low. In this paper the high tone is shown with a macron over the vowel, as /ā/, and the low tone by the bare vowel, as /a/.

new_statements.relation_note: First-hand: Laya seems to have a high/low two-tone contrast; all vocabulary is transcribed with this tone marking. No consonant/vowel inventory section and no stress statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Two-way (high vs low) tone register on syllables, marked per vowel in the author's field transcription; the author hedges ('there appear to be'); nothing is said about word stress/accent.
new_statements.exceptions: none; statement is tentative ('あるようである' = 'there appear to be'), based on a 3.5-hour elicitation session with two speakers
new_statements.identity_note: Explicitly 'ラヤ語 (Layakha)', the speech of the Laya (ラヤ族) yak herders of Gasa district, northern Bhutan, classed as a kind of Dzongkha close to Tibetan (citing van Driem 1998); consultants: a 60-year-old woman and her 61-year-old husband from Laya village, Gasa, interviewed in Punakha on 26 Feb 2019. Matches laya1253 / ISO lya exactly; not Lunana (luk) or Lingzhi.

sources.citation: Tournadre, Nicolas & Hiroyuki Suzuki. 2023. The Tibetic Languages: An introduction to the family of languages derived from Old Tibetan. Villejuif: LACITO-Publications. 1151 pp.
sources.note: Nothing for Laya. Ch. 9.7.2 p. 555 says Laya, Lingzhi and Lunana are three yakherd varieties of Dzongkha that 'have so far not been studied'; p. 557 and App. 3 p. 1033 only locate Laya (Dzongkha dialect 72.1, map I7). The book's stress discussion (sec. 7.3.3-7.3.4, pp. 241-243) concerns Lhasa/Amdo etc. a full-text search for stress/accent the full text for 'Laya' (excluding 'Himalaya') yields only these three passages.

sources.citation: Tshering, Karma & George van Driem. 2019. The Grammar of Dzongkha: Revised and Expanded. Santa Barbara: Himalayan Linguistics. (revision of van Driem & Tshering 1998, Dzongkha, Languages of the Greater Himalayan Region 1)
sources.note: Nothing for Laya. Ch. 1 p. 4: 'Peculiar dialects of Dzongkha are spoken in the far north, viz. the dialect of the alpine yakherd communities of 'Lingzhi, Laya and Lunana.. Much of the couleur locale of these northern dialects results from structural and lexical similarities with Tibetan.' The phonology is explicitly 'based on a single prestige variety' (Wang/Thê); no other Laya mentions apart from example sentences and a place-name list.

sources.note: Nothing for Laya: 'Layakha' occurs only in the gloss of a text example (p. 165, ex. 42a, a speaker saying Layakha words cannot be understood). Stress statements there are about standard Dzongkha.

sources.citation: Chamberlain, Brad. 2015. Linguistic watersheds: a model for understanding variation among the Tibetic languages. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society (JSEALS) 8: 71-96. Canberra: Asia-Pacific Linguistics. (CC-BY)
sources.note: Nothing. Classification by watershed only; p. 88: 'I have not yet seen any linguistic data from any of these varieties. However, anecdotally, within Bhutan, the Laya language is seen to be quite similar to Dzongkha'. Quotes Tournadre 2014 that 'some of these [Tibetic] languages are tonal, while others are nontonal' (p. 73) without assigning Laya.
